title: Author Tone and Attitude in RC
tagline: Year 3 — Reading word choice, qualifiers and irony to name the author's attitude

introduction.overview: Tone is the author's attitude towards the subject, shown not by what is said but by how it is said. Adjectives, adverbs, qualifiers, rhetorical questions and irony all carry attitude. Tone questions ask you to name that attitude (sceptical, appreciative, urgent, neutral) or to say what a phrase is meant to convey. The skill is to read the choice of words, not just the facts.
introduction.placementRelevance: Tone and attitude questions appear in nearly every advanced reading-comprehension set.
introduction.realWorldContext: Telling whether an email is polite, irritated or sarcastic depends on the same cues.

learningObjectives: Identify positive, negative and neutral tone
Avoid extreme tone labels for balanced passages

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A tone word should fit most of the passage, not just one sentence. Balanced passages call for balanced tone words.

coreDefinitions: Tone: the author's attitude to the subject.
Irony: saying one thing and meaning another, often the opposite.
Concession: admitting a weakness before making the main point ("not flawless, but…").
Loaded word: a word that carries approval or disapproval (transformative, blemishes).
Neutral tone: informative and unemotional, with few evaluative words.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Ask what the author wants you to feel about the subject, and which words push you that way.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Underline evaluative words. Decide positive, negative or mixed. Choose the tone word that fits the strongest evidence and the amount of emotion shown.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Irony pattern
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Praise word in doubtful context ⇒ sarcasm

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Intensity check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Match strength of tone word to strength of text

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Whole-passage check
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: One sentence is not the tone

mainNarrative: In the annual-report passage, the report calls the year "transformative", but the author lists the facts it leaves out: costs rose faster than revenue, managers resigned and a key product has no customers. The final sentence says the report records "a skilful rearrangement of adjectives". The tone is sceptical and ironic.

The novel passage opens with a concession: the middle drags and minor characters are thin. Then "but" turns to "rare generosity" and a final scene "as moving as anything written in the past decade". The tone is appreciative, with minor reservations.
The river passage uses short, strong sentences and a blunt closing line. The author is urgent and critical of delay, calling it "a decision to let the valley die".
To choose between close tone words, calibrate intensity. "Critical" fits mild disapproval; "scornful" fits contempt. Choose the word that matches how strong the text feels.
A balanced passage deserves a balanced tone word, such as "measured" or "appreciative but not uncritical", not an extreme one.

deepDiveAspects.title: Irony with quotation marks
deepDiveAspects.content: Scare quotes around a word such as "transformative" signal that the author does not accept it.

deepDiveAspects.title: Concession before conclusion
deepDiveAspects.content: The strongest clause in a "not X, but Y" sentence is Y.

solvedExamples.title: Irony
solvedExamples.question: A report calls the year "transformative", yet costs rose faster than revenue. The author calls it "a skilful rearrangement of adjectives". What is the tone?

steps.title: Mismatch
steps.explanation: The word "transformative" is not supported by the facts.

steps.title: Tone
steps.explanation: The author doubts the report: sceptical and ironic.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The author does not accept the claim.

solvedExamples.title: Concession
solvedExamples.question: A reviewer says a novel is "not flawless" but "a work of rare generosity". What is the reviewer's attitude?

solvedExamples.title: Urgency
solvedExamples.question: An author says that waiting for more studies is "a decision to let the valley die". What is the tone?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: It is impassioned rather than calm.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Underline evaluative words, check for irony and concessions, then choose the tone word that matches the strength of the evidence.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate tone words that do not fit the majority of the passage.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Look at the last sentence; it often states the tone openly.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Neutral options are right only when the text has no evaluative words.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The company's annual report describes the year as "transformative". Revenue did rise by two per cent, but the report neglects to mention that costs rose by six, that three senior managers resigned, and that the new product on which the strategy depends has yet to find a single paying customer. A transformation, one might think, requires something to have changed. What the report really records is a skilful rearrangement of adjectives.

The author's attitude towards the company's report is
easy.explanation: The author lists facts the report leaves out and ends with an ironic remark, which shows doubt about the report.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Her last novel is not flawless; the middle chapters drag and a few of the minor characters are barely sketched. But these are small blemishes in a work of rare generosity. Every character, even the villain, is allowed to be right about something, and the final scene, in which two old rivals share a quiet meal, is as moving as anything written in the past decade.

The author's attitude towards the novel is
easy.explanation: The review admits small flaws but calls the work "rare generosity" and the last scene deeply moving.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The river that supplied this valley for ten thousand years now fails in the dry season. The wells are going deeper, the fields are going brown and the young are leaving. We are told to wait for studies. But the studies were done long ago and they say the same thing: the water is being taken faster than it returns. Further delay is not caution; it is a decision to let the valley die.

The author's tone is best described as
easy.explanation: Short, strong statements and the description of delay as a decision to let the valley die show urgency and criticism.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Her last novel is not flawless; the middle chapters drag and a few of the minor characters are barely sketched. But these are small blemishes in a work of rare generosity. Every character, even the villain, is allowed to be right about something, and the final scene, in which two old rivals share a quiet meal, is as moving as anything written in the past decade.

The word "but" in the second sentence signals
options: a shift from praise to reservations
a contradiction of the first sentence
a shift from reservations to praise
intermediate.correctAnswer: a shift from reservations to praise
intermediate.explanation: The first sentence lists faults; "but" turns to the novel's strengths.

Read the passage and answer the question.

We are told to wait for studies. But the studies were done long ago and they say the same thing: the water is being taken faster than it returns. Which of the following best describes how the tone changes in the passage?
options: It moves from anger to calm acceptance
It moves from humour to sadness
It moves from describing a problem to blunt criticism of inaction
advanced.correctAnswer: It moves from describing a problem to blunt criticism of inaction
advanced.explanation: The passage first describes the failing river and its effects, then criticises waiting for further studies.
